walkthroughs.body_html:
[Cu(H2O)6]^2+ + 4NH3 (after deprotonation) -> [Cu(NH3)4(H2O)2]^2+ (deep blue). 6-coord retained.

[Cu(H2O)6]^2+ + 4Cl- -> [CuCl4]^2- (yellow). Coordination drops from 6 to 4 (larger Cl-, geometry change).

Replacing 6 H2O with 3 bidentate ligands releases 6 H2O molecules but uses 3 new ligands -> entropy rises.

ΔG more negative due to +ΔS, so chelated complex more stable. EDTA traps metal in single 6-coord chelate.

Fe^2+ in haemoglobin reversibly binds O2. CO binds ~200x more strongly than O2 -> dangerous as it does not release.

This is a ligand substitution: O2 displaced by CO. CN- also strongly binds, poisoning cytochromes.

mcqs.q: Why is EDTA complex very stable?
Why does the colour of a transition metal complex change when ligands are exchanged?
options: Different ligands cause different amounts of d-orbital splitting, so different wavelengths of light are absorbed.
The colour changes because the new ligand is itself coloured.
The ligand shares electrons equally with the metal as a normal covalent bond.
The colour changes because the metal ion itself changes oxidation state.

mcqs.q: What kind of bond forms between a ligand and a central metal ion in a complex?
options: Transition metals are coloured because their nuclei emit photons in the visible range.
The ligand forms an ionic bond with the metal because the metal is positively charged.
A dative (coordinate) covalent bond — the ligand donates a lone pair into an empty orbital on the metal.
The ligand shares electrons equally with the metal as a normal covalent bond.

mcqs.q: Why are most transition metal complex ions coloured?
options: Transition metal ions are coloured because they have a half-full d-subshell which naturally absorbs light.
Ligands split the d-orbitals into two energy levels; electrons absorb visible light to jump between them (d-d transitions), and the complementary colour is transmitted.
The colour changes because the new ligand is itself coloured.
Transition metals are coloured because their nuclei emit photons in the visible range.
